section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Basis Vectors
section_1.content: Briefly recap 3D space defined by unit vectors î (1,0,0), ĵ (0,1,0), and k̂ (0,0,1). Emphasize that any vector in space is a combination of these.
section_1.example: Imagine a 3D grid cube. Point to the three edges starting from the origin as the 'anchors' of our coordinate system.

section_2.title: Defining Linear Transformation
section_2.content: Introduce transformations as 'moving' space. A transformation is linear if grid lines remain parallel and evenly spaced, and the origin remains fixed.
section_2.example: Visualize a 3D block of jelly being stretched and tilted while keeping the bottom corner (origin) nailed to the floor.

section_3.title: The Transformation Matrix (The 'Recipe')
section_3.content: Explain that we only need to know where î, ĵ, and k̂ land to define the entire transformation. These three destination vectors form the columns of a 3x3 matrix.
section_3.example: A 'Robot Arm' character: The arm's transformation is defined by where its X, Y, and Z axes point after it moves.

section_4.title: Visualizing Rotation and Scaling
section_4.content: Demonstrate the matrix multiplication process. Scaling alters the length of the basis vectors; rotation changes their direction while maintaining their orthogonality.
section_4.example: A game character model: Applying a Scaling Matrix to make the character 'grow' (all vectors lengthen) vs. a Rotation Matrix to make the character 'turn'.

section_5.title: Determinants: The Volume Factor
section_5.content: Explain the determinant of the 3x3 matrix as the factor by which the transformation scales the volume of space.
section_5.example: A unit cube containing a 'Space Cat'. After transformation, the determinant tells us how much the 'cat's' occupied volume has expanded or shrunk.
